For instance, in 2024, Chinese PV manufacturer JinkoSolar donated solar modules to Tribes in Montana and South Dakota (Fischer 2025)—states that host intercontinental ballistic missile fields and one of the U.S. Air Force’s two B-1B Lancer wings. In addition, an anticipated shortage of offshore wind turbine installation vessels by the late 2020s (WindEurope 2025c) could create an opportunity for China to gain access to strategically important regions worldwide. Working with local authorities and international partners will be key to preventing surveillance opportunities. 4.1.4 U.S. Influence More generally, adversaries could leverage their contributions to advanced energy technologies and manufacturing to undermine U.S. influence, potentially degrading DOW interests, such as in area/port access, basing, and overflight. By promoting itself as a leader in energy manufacturing, adoption, and research and development, China could challenge U.S. leadership in the energy technology space (Russell 2024; Geall and Ely 2018). For example, China’s status as a leader in advanced energy technologies could give China more influence in international forums and bilateral engagements, such as at a United Nations-organized meeting in April 2025 when Chinese President Xi Jinping and European Commission President von der Leyen joined other global leaders (absent U.S. representation) in reaffirming international commitment to climate action (Millan, Ainger, and Iglesias 2025). U.S. engagement would need to offer these countries more than Chinese energy investment does, and DOW may want to work with other U.S. federal partners to determine tailored mitigation opportunities by country. Contingency planning and deepening partnerships with foreign partners could also help mitigate this risk. 4.2 Competition for Innovative Technologies Research and development into advanced energy technologies continues around the world, and adversaries could gain the upper hand on the battlefield and secure a strategic lead for years to come if they are the first to deploy new technologies at scale, especially potentially disruptive technologies, such as power beaming, point-of-need marine and hydrokinetic energy (i.e., a power source that is harnessed from the natural movement of water, including waves, tides, and river and ocean currents), solid-state batteries, point-of-need hydrogen production, and small modular (i.e., nuclear) reactors. A historical parallel can be seen in the early 20th-century shift from coal to oil-powered naval fleets, which gave nations like the United Kingdom and the United States a decisive operational advantage over coal-dependent rivals (Yergin 1991). China’s leadership in research and development and in translating energy innovations to commercialization, in part due to its control over supply chains and access to critical minerals and its established and interconnected manufacturing infrastructure, positions the country as the United States’ primary competition for innovative energy technologies.
